title: System design for CRUD apps
blurb: Caches, queues, background jobs, file storage, email, webhooks, multi-tenancy and scaling a monolith: the design round for product-engineering roles, without the FAANG theatre.

questions.q: What is the difference between cache-aside and write-through caching?
choices: Cache-aside keeps the cache on a separate server; write-through keeps it inside the database
Cache-aside fills the cache on a read miss; write-through updates the cache on every write
Cache-aside never expires its entries; write-through expires them as soon as the row changes
Cache-aside buffers writes until a batch is flushed; write-through sends each write straight on
questions.why: Cache-aside loads lazily, so it only caches what is read, and entries go stale until invalidated or expired. Write-through keeps the cache fresh on every write, at the cost of caching data nobody reads. Buffering writes for later is write-behind, a third pattern.
questions.asked: The opening move of most caching discussions; the follow-up is how each one goes stale.

questions.q: Product prices are cached for 10 minutes, so after an admin edits a price customers see the old one for up to 10 minutes. What removes that delay?
choices: Delete or update the cache entry in the same code path that saves the new price
Lower the TTL to 10 seconds, which makes the cached price effectively always fresh
Move the cache into the database server, so it sees each update the moment it lands
Store the prices as strings in the cache, so a changed value is detected on read
questions.why: Explicit invalidation on write removes the stale window; the TTL stays as a safety net for missed invalidations. A 10-second TTL only shrinks the window and multiplies database load by sixty.
questions.asked: Checks that you know 'there are only two hard things' is about this, and have an answer beyond a shorter TTL.

questions.q: A popular cache key expires, and hundreds of concurrent requests miss at once and all query the database. What prevents this stampede?
choices: Give the key a longer TTL, so the database is hit less often when it does expire
Let one request rebuild the value while the others wait for it or get the stale copy
Add a read replica, so the burst of identical queries is spread over two databases
Shorten the TTL, so each expiry releases a smaller burst of requests on the database
questions.why: Request coalescing (a lock or single-flight per key), serving stale while one caller refreshes, or refreshing early with jitter all make one query do the work of hundreds. A longer TTL only makes the stampede rarer; a replica halves it.
questions.asked: A production-scar question; people who have seen a stampede describe single-flight or stale-while-revalidate.

questions.q: Your CDN caches `GET /api/me/orders`, and users start seeing each other's orders. What went wrong?
choices: The CDN's TTL was too long; a TTL under a minute would keep each user's data apart
The CDN's edge servers share a disk, so all users on one edge location read the same stored file
A per-user response was cacheable by shared caches; it needs `private` or `no-store`
The API returned an ETag, and matching ETags let the CDN swap users' responses
questions.why: Shared caches key on the URL, and `/me/orders` is the same URL for everyone. Personal responses must say `Cache-Control: private` (browser only) or `no-store`. A short TTL just leaks for less time.
questions.asked: A real incident class; it tests whether you think about who else a cache serves.

questions.q: A public product catalogue page is the same for every visitor and changes a few times a day. Where does caching it help most?
choices: At the CDN edge, so most requests never reach your servers at all
In each app instance's memory, so every server keeps its own private copy
In the database's buffer cache, which keeps the hottest table pages in RAM
In the browser's localStorage, written by a script on each page view
questions.why: Cache as close to the user as the data allows: public, rarely changing content belongs at the edge, and a purge on change keeps it fresh. An in-process cache still costs a request per visitor and is per instance, and localStorage helps only repeat visits by one person.
questions.asked: Tests whether you pick a cache layer from the data, not from habit.

questions.q: Why put a message queue between the web app and the service that generates PDF invoices?
choices: A queue makes each PDF render faster, because messages are processed in memory
The request returns quickly, and bursts are absorbed and worked off at the worker's pace
A queue guarantees each invoice is generated exactly once, even if a worker crashes midway
A queue lets the web app read the finished PDF in the same request that asked for it
questions.why: The queue decouples the two: the web tier stays responsive, a spike becomes a backlog instead of an outage, and the worker can be down briefly without losing work. Most queues deliver at least once, so exactly-once is not what you get.
questions.asked: The first question in any async-work discussion; "smoothing spikes" is the phrase interviewers listen for.

questions.q: Your queue delivers at least once, and a 'charge card' message is occasionally processed twice. What is the standard fix?
choices: Switch the queue to exactly-once mode, which removes every duplicate on the broker
Acknowledge the message before processing, so it can never be delivered again
Make the consumer idempotent, for example by recording processed message ids
Delay each charge briefly so the duplicate arrives first and can be dropped
questions.why: At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer gives effectively-once effects: store the message id (or pass an idempotency key to the payment provider) and skip repeats. Acknowledging first turns it into at-most-once, so a crash loses the charge.
questions.asked: The single most important queue fact; candidates who say "exactly once" without caveats get probed hard.

questions.q: What is a dead-letter queue for?
choices: Storing messages for consumers that are offline, until they come back online
Archiving every processed message, so the full history can be replayed later
Holding messages that failed processing too many times, so they can be inspected
Delaying messages that are scheduled to be processed at a later time of day, such as reminders
questions.why: After a set number of failed deliveries the broker moves the message aside, so it stops blocking or burning the consumer. Someone must alert on it and replay or discard its contents; a DLQ nobody watches is silent data loss.
questions.asked: A vocabulary check; the strong answer adds "and alert on it".

questions.q: You save an order, then publish an OrderPlaced event; if the process dies between the two, the event is lost. What does the outbox pattern do?
choices: Publishes the event first and saves the order only once the broker confirms receipt
Saves the event in an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay publishes it later
Wraps the database write and the broker publish together in one two-phase commit
Retries the publish in a loop inside the request until the broker finally accepts it
questions.why: The order and its event commit or roll back together, and a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes, retrying until it succeeds. Consumers may see a duplicate, so they stay idempotent. Publishing first just moves the gap, and two-phase commit across a DB and a broker is what the outbox avoids.
questions.asked: A mid-to-senior design question; naming the dual-write problem before the pattern is the strong answer.

questions.q: One malformed message makes the consumer throw every time, and the queue keeps redelivering it. What should the consumer setup do?
choices: Retry it forever with exponential backoff, since the bug will eventually be fixed
Delete it silently on the first failure, so it can never block the queue again
Restart the consumer process after each failure, which clears the bad state
Cap delivery attempts, then move the message to a dead-letter queue and alert
questions.why: A poison message never succeeds, so unbounded retries waste capacity and can block ordered queues. Capping attempts and dead-lettering keeps the message for diagnosis. Deleting on the first failure also throws away messages that failed for a transient reason.
questions.asked: Tests whether you separate transient failures from permanent ones in a consumer.

questions.q: Several consumers process order events in parallel, but events for the same order must be handled in sequence. What is the usual approach?
choices: Partition by order id, so every event for one order reaches the same consumer in order
Add a timestamp to each event and have consumers sleep until earlier ones finish
Use one consumer for the whole queue, since that is the only way to keep any order
Let any consumer take any event, and sort the order's history in the database later
questions.why: Ordering is needed per key, not globally, so partitioning by key (Kafka partitions, SQS FIFO message groups, Service Bus sessions) keeps parallelism across orders. A single consumer works but throws away all throughput.
questions.asked: Checks whether you know ordering is a per-key property you design for.

questions.q: Users upload videos of up to 2 GB. Which design keeps that traffic off your API servers?
choices: Stream each upload through the API and write it into a binary column in the database
The API hands out a short-lived pre-signed URL; the browser uploads straight to storage
Raise the API's body-size limit and request timeout, then scale the API out to cope
Split the file into chunks in the browser and post all of the chunks to the API in parallel
questions.why: A pre-signed URL grants time-limited permission to write one object, so the bytes go from browser to object storage while your API only authorises and records the key. Chunking through the API still pushes every byte through your servers.
questions.asked: A standard design-round step; the follow-up is how you know the upload finished.

questions.q: Why do most CRUD apps keep uploaded files in object storage and only a key in the database?
choices: Databases cannot store binary data reliably, so files have to live somewhere else
Blobs bloat backups and database memory, while object storage is cheap and serves files
Object storage encrypts every file automatically, which a relational database cannot do
Storing files in the database breaks foreign keys whenever a file is replaced
questions.why: Databases can hold blobs, but they then swell backups, replication and the buffer cache, and every download costs a database connection. Object storage is priced for bytes and can serve files directly or through a CDN.
questions.asked: A junior design check; the strong answer mentions backups and serving files through a CDN.

questions.q: After upload, each image needs a thumbnail and a malware scan. Where should that work run?
choices: Inside the upload request itself, so the user waits and then sees the thumbnail at once
In the browser before upload, so the server receives a thumbnail and a clean file
In a background worker fired by an upload event, with the file marked pending meanwhile
In a nightly batch job, which processes all of the day's uploads in one efficient run
questions.why: Slow, failure-prone work belongs in a worker that can retry, while the file stays unusable until the scan passes. The browser cannot be trusted to scan its own upload, and a nightly batch leaves files unscanned for hours.
questions.asked: Combines storage and background work; the "pending until scanned" state is the detail interviewers want.

questions.q: Why do apps send transactional email through a queue and an email provider rather than over SMTP inside the request?
choices: SMTP cannot send HTML email, so a provider is needed to format the message body
Email providers deliver instantly, while SMTP servers batch messages once an hour
The request stays fast, and a failed send is retried without the user resubmitting
Browsers block requests that open SMTP connections, so the server must hand them off
questions.why: Mail servers are slow and sometimes down, so sending inline makes signup slow and fragile. A queued send retries on its own, and a provider handles deliverability, bounces and sender reputation.
questions.asked: A small design question that shows whether you move slow side effects out of the request by default.

questions.q: Your app sends webhooks to customer endpoints, which are sometimes down. What should the sender do?
choices: Retry immediately in a tight loop until the endpoint responds, so no event is late
Send each event once and drop it on failure, since the customer can poll the API
Block the business action that caused the event until the customer's endpoint accepts it
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and keep a delivery log customers can replay
questions.why: Backoff with jitter gives a struggling endpoint room to recover, and a delivery log with status and replay lets customers recover from long outages themselves. Tying your own transaction to a customer's uptime makes their outage yours.
questions.asked: Tests whether you design for the other side being unreliable, which is always true of webhooks.

questions.q: You are building a SaaS app for thousands of small customers. Which tenancy model is the usual starting point?
choices: A database per tenant, so each customer's data is fully isolated from day one
A schema per tenant, so each customer gets its own tables inside one database
One shared schema, with a tenant_id column on every tenant-owned table
One app deployment per tenant, each with its own database and its own domain
questions.why: A shared schema is the cheapest to run: one migration, one connection pool, easy cross-tenant reporting. Thousands of databases or schemas multiply migrations and connections. The price is that isolation depends on every query filtering by tenant.
questions.asked: The standard SaaS design question; strong answers name the operational cost of the isolated options.

questions.q: In a shared-schema multi-tenant app, what stops one forgotten `WHERE tenant_id = …` from leaking data?
choices: Applying the tenant filter centrally, such as an ORM global filter or row-level security
Asking reviewers to check every new query for a tenant clause during each code review
Hiding tenant ids from the client, so users can never guess or enumerate another tenant's id
Giving each tenant its own API key, so requests only reach their own data
questions.why: Make the safe path the default: an EF Core global query filter or Postgres row-level security adds the tenant condition to every query automatically. Review helps but misses one query eventually, and hiding ids does nothing when a query forgets the filter.
questions.asked: Checks whether you rely on discipline or on design for your most dangerous bug class.

questions.q: One tenant's nightly export saturates the shared database and slows every other tenant. What handles this noisy neighbour without buying capacity for one tenant's peak?
choices: Per-tenant quotas and rate limits, with heavy exports moved to a queue and a replica
A larger database instance, so there is always spare capacity for every tenant
An index on tenant_id, so every tenant's queries run faster regardless of load
Separate login pages per tenant, so their traffic arrives through different routes
questions.why: Isolate the heavy workload: throttle per tenant, and run exports as background jobs against a replica so they cannot starve interactive traffic. A bigger instance buys time until the next export grows. Very large tenants may eventually get their own database.
questions.asked: A senior-leaning SaaS question; the strong answer separates interactive and batch workloads.

questions.q: A large enterprise customer requires its own database, while your other tenants share one. What does this hybrid cost you?
choices: Nothing extra; the ORM routes queries to the right database without any changes
Tenant-aware connection routing, and running every migration against each database
The shared tenants must move to their own databases too, since models cannot mix
Cross-tenant reports become impossible, because one SQL query cannot read from two databases
questions.why: You now resolve the tenant before opening a connection, and every migration and backup must run per database. Cross-tenant reporting gets harder (usually via a warehouse), but it is not impossible, and the shared tenants can stay as they are.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can price a sales request in engineering terms.

questions.q: Your single-server app slows as traffic grows, and nothing is badly tuned. What is usually the cheapest first step?
choices: Split the app into microservices so that each part can be scaled on its own
Scale vertically: move to a bigger instance, which needs no code changes
Rewrite the hottest paths in a faster language before adding any hardware
Shard the database by customer, so each shard holds a fraction of the data
questions.why: A bigger machine is a config change, and modern instances go a long way. Scale out when you need redundancy or hit the ceiling. Microservices and sharding add permanent complexity to solve a problem you may not have yet.
questions.asked: Checks for pragmatism; jumping to microservices is the answer that worries interviewers.

questions.q: Why must app servers be stateless before you put several of them behind a load balancer?
choices: Any instance can serve any request, because sessions and files live in shared stores
Stateless servers use less memory, so the load balancer can pack more onto a host
Load balancers refuse to route traffic to servers holding data in local memory
Stateless servers never need a database, so they can be copied without running any migrations
questions.why: If a session or uploaded file lives on one server, the next request may land elsewhere and find nothing. Sticky sessions paper over it but break on deploys and uneven load. Move sessions, files and caches that must be shared to shared stores.
questions.asked: A foundation for every scaling discussion; the strong answer mentions why sticky sessions are a crutch.

questions.q: Reads go to a read replica. A user saves their profile, the page reloads, and it shows the old values. Why?
choices: The replica caches query results and only refreshes them every few minutes
Replication is asynchronous, so the replica briefly lags behind the primary
The write went to the replica and was rejected, since replicas are read-only
The ORM reuses the first connection it opened, which still sees the old data
questions.why: The write is committed on the primary and reaches the replica a moment later. For read-your-writes, send that user's reads to the primary for a short window after a write, or read from the primary for pages that follow a save.
questions.asked: Replicas are the first scaling step for reads; lag is the catch every interviewer checks you know.

questions.q: You scale from 4 to 40 app instances, each with a pool of 50 connections, and Postgres starts refusing connections. What is the usual fix?
choices: Raise the Postgres `max_connections` to 2,000 so every instance pool fits
Put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front of Postgres and shrink each app pool
Remove the app-side pools so each request opens and closes its own connection
Add a read replica, so half of the connections go to a second database server
questions.why: Each Postgres connection is a process with its own memory, so thousands of mostly idle connections hurt performance. A pooler multiplexes many client connections onto a few server ones. Dropping app pools makes it worse, and a replica only helps reads.
questions.asked: A real scaling wall; people who have hit it name PgBouncer or an equivalent immediately.

questions.q: A team of six is starting a new product. Why is a modular monolith usually preferred over microservices?
choices: Monoliths scale better under load, because function calls are faster than HTTP calls
Microservices need a separate database technology per service, which six people cannot run
Microservices cannot share one code repository, so each service needs its own team
Clear module boundaries without network calls, distributed failures or many pipelines
questions.why: You keep the design benefit (boundaries you can later extract along) without paying for network calls, partial failures, distributed data and many deploys. Microservices solve team-scaling problems a team of six does not have. Monorepos with many services are common.
questions.asked: A judgement question; interviewers want to hear the cost of microservices, not their brochure.

questions.q: A list endpoint over 50 million rows is slow mainly because it returns an exact total count with every page. What is the usual fix?
choices: Cache the total count forever, since the table grows too slowly for it to matter
Drop the exact total: return 'has more', or an estimate, and count only when asked
Add an index on every filter column, which makes COUNT(*) instant even on very big tables
Switch to offset pagination, which returns the total count free with each page
questions.why: An exact count over a filtered large table still visits every matching row or index entry, on every page. Most UIs only need "next page exists", which you get by fetching one extra row, or an approximate count from planner statistics.
questions.asked: Tests whether you question a requirement that is expensive at scale.

questions.q: A downstream service is timing out, and your retries are making its recovery harder. What does a circuit breaker add?
choices: It retries each failed call straight away, several times, until one succeeds
It routes the calls to a cached copy of the service kept on the calling side
After repeated failures it fails fast for a cool-off period instead of calling
It raises the timeout on each call, so slow responses stop counting as failures
questions.why: Once failures pass a threshold the breaker opens and calls fail immediately, then a trial call tests recovery. That stops your retries from piling onto a struggling service and frees your own threads. Pair it with timeouts and backoff, and a fallback where you have one.
questions.asked: Checks whether you know retries can cause outages, and what stops them.

questions.q: Anonymous bots hammer your public search endpoint. Where is it cheapest to reject the excess traffic?
choices: In the database, with a statement timeout that cancels queries past a limit
Inside each controller action, after the request is authenticated and parsed
In the browser, by disabling the search button for a few seconds after each search is run
At the edge, in the CDN, gateway or load balancer, before requests reach the app
questions.why: Every layer a request passes costs you, so coarse per-IP limits belong at the edge. Per-user and per-plan limits still live in the app, backed by a shared counter. Bots do not use your UI, so a disabled button stops nobody.
questions.asked: A placement question; the strong answer layers edge limits with app-level per-user limits.

questions.q: What does a cache's hit ratio tell you?
choices: How many keys the cache can hold before it starts evicting the oldest ones
What share of lookups were served from the cache instead of the source
How long, on average, each entry survives before its TTL expires
How much faster a cached read is than the equivalent database query
questions.why: Hit ratio is hits divided by total lookups. A cache with a 20% hit ratio adds a network hop to 80% of requests and saves little, so it is the first number to check. Capacity, TTL and speed-up are separate measures that influence the ratio but are not it.
questions.asked: Checks you judge a cache by evidence rather than assuming it helps; strong answers say what ratio would make them remove it.

questions.q: `GET /api/products?category=shoes&sort=price&page=2` is cached in Redis. Which cache key is correct?
choices: `products` alone, since every page reads the same product table underneath
`products:page:2`, since the page number is what changes between requests
`products:shoes`, since the category is the only filter that narrows the rows
`products:shoes:price:2`, built from every parameter that changes the result
questions.why: The key must include every input that changes the response, otherwise two different queries share one entry and users see the wrong list. Keying on the page or category alone serves page 2 of a price sort to someone asking for page 2 sorted by name.
questions.asked: Wrong keys are the most common real caching bug, and they only show up once two users ask slightly different questions.

questions.q: After updating a product in the database, why do teams usually delete its cache key rather than write the new value into the cache?
choices: Deleting is faster in Redis than overwriting a key with a new serialised value
Two concurrent writers can set the cache out of order, leaving an old value in place
Writing to the cache would require a distributed transaction with the database
A deleted key is repopulated with a fresh TTL, which a written value would not get
questions.why: If writer A and writer B both update the row and then set the cache, A's set can land after B's and leave A's older value cached indefinitely. Deleting lets the next read fetch whatever the database holds now. Speed is not the reason, and a set can carry a TTL just as easily.
questions.asked: Interviewers want the race described, not just the rule; it shows you think about concurrent requests.

questions.q: With cache-aside, a reader misses, loads the old row, and is paused; meanwhile a writer updates the row and deletes the key; then the reader stores the old row. What bounds how long this stale entry lives?
choices: The TTL on the entry, which is why cache-aside entries should always have one
Nothing, because the writer's delete already ran and will not run again
Redis detects that the key was deleted recently and rejects the late write
The database transaction isolation level, which prevents the reader from seeing old data
questions.why: This interleaving is rare but real, and the writer's delete has already happened, so only expiry will clear it. That is why every cache-aside entry gets a TTL even when you also invalidate on write. Redis does not remember deletions, and isolation levels govern the database read, not what the reader later puts in the cache.
questions.asked: Separates people who have read about invalidation from people who have debugged it; the TTL-as-safety-net answer is what they want.

questions.q: Your API runs as three instances, each with an in-process memory cache of product data. An admin edits a product. What happens?
choices: All three caches update, because they share the process's configuration
Only the instance that handled the edit can invalidate its own copy
The load balancer forwards the invalidation to the other two instances
The edit fails until all three instances acknowledge the new value
questions.why: An in-process cache lives in one process's memory, so the other two keep serving the old value until their TTL expires. That is the usual reason to move to a shared cache such as Redis, or to broadcast invalidations over pub/sub. Load balancers route requests; they know nothing about your cache.
questions.asked: A classic scaling-out surprise; the good answer names both fixes: a shared cache or a short TTL you can live with.

questions.q: Bots request `/api/users/<random-id>` for IDs that do not exist, and every request reaches the database. Which caching technique helps?
choices: Caching the 404 result for those IDs for a short time
Raising the TTL on the entries for users that do exist
Warming the cache with every user ID on application start
Switching from cache-aside to write-through for the users
questions.why: Negative caching stores "not found" with a short TTL, so repeated misses for the same ID stop reaching the database. Longer TTLs and write-through only help keys that exist. Preloading every user wastes memory and still misses the random IDs; rate limiting is the other half of the answer.
questions.asked: Shows you know caches can protect the database from misses, not only speed up hits.

questions.q: Why add random jitter to cache TTLs, for example 600 seconds plus or minus 60?
choices: So that keys written together do not all expire at the same moment
So that Redis spreads the keys more evenly across its memory pages
So that attackers cannot predict when a sensitive entry will change
So that each application instance ends up with a slightly different copy
questions.why: A cache warmed in one burst, such as after a deploy, would otherwise expire in one burst and send every key's miss to the database at once. Jitter smears those expiries out. It has nothing to do with Redis memory layout or with security.
questions.asked: A small detail that signals you have seen a cache cause an outage rather than prevent one.

questions.q: What does `Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300` allow a CDN or browser to do?
choices: Revalidate with the origin on every request but skip the body if unchanged
Serve the cached copy for 60 s, then serve it stale while refetching in the background
Keep the response for 360 s and then discard it without contacting the origin
Cache the response only when the origin sent it within the last 300 seconds
questions.why: For 60 seconds the copy is fresh. For the next 300 it may be served immediately while a background request fetches a new one, so users never wait on the origin. Revalidating on every request is `no-cache`, which is the usual confusion.
questions.asked: A good answer mentions that this hides origin latency from users while keeping content only slightly behind.

questions.q: Each user's permissions are cached for 15 minutes. An admin removes someone's access. What is the right way to make that take effect quickly?
choices: Lower the TTL for every user's permissions to a few seconds
Flush the entire cache whenever any role assignment changes
Delete that user's permission key in the code that changes roles
Ask the user to sign out and back in so their cache is rebuilt
questions.why: Invalidate the specific key at the point of change, and keep the TTL as a backstop. A tiny TTL for everyone throws away most of the cache's value; flushing everything causes a stampede; relying on the user to sign out means a removed employee keeps access.
questions.asked: Permission caches are where stale data becomes a security issue; interviewers look for targeted invalidation.

questions.q: Your Redis cache becomes unreachable. How should a well-built CRUD API behave?
choices: Return 503 until Redis is back, since serving uncached data is inconsistent
Restart the application instances so they reconnect to Redis on startup
Queue incoming reads until Redis responds, then serve them in order
Fall back to the database with a short cache timeout and log the failure
questions.why: A cache is an optimisation, so losing it should make the app slower, not broken. A short timeout on cache calls stops every request hanging on a dead Redis. Failing requests or queueing reads turns an optional component into a single point of failure, and restarts do not fix an unreachable server.
questions.asked: Interviewers probe whether you treat the cache as optional; the follow-up is usually whether the database can survive the extra load.

questions.q: What is a read replica in a relational database setup?
choices: A copy kept in sync from the primary that serves read-only queries
A second primary that accepts writes and merges them with the first
A nightly backup restored onto another server for reporting jobs
A cache layer in front of the database that stores recent query results
questions.why: A replica receives the primary's changes, usually asynchronously, and can answer reads so the primary handles fewer queries. It does not accept writes; multi-primary replication is a different, harder setup. A nightly restore is a snapshot, not a replica.
questions.asked: Vocabulary for the scaling part of the design round; the good answer mentions replication lag in the same breath.

questions.q: Reads go to an asynchronous replica, and users complain that their own edits vanish after saving. Which fix keeps most reads on the replica?
choices: Switch the replica to synchronous replication so it is never behind
Send all reads back to the primary and remove the replica entirely
Route a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after they write
Add a one-second delay after every save before returning the response
questions.why: Read-your-writes only matters for the user who just wrote, so pinning that user to the primary briefly fixes it and leaves other reads on the replica. Synchronous replication slows every write, dropping the replica removes the benefit, and a fixed delay guesses at the lag.
questions.asked: The follow-up to 'why is it stale'; interviewers want a targeted fix rather than abandoning the replica.

questions.q: Why is adding more API instances usually easier than adding more database servers?
choices: Stateless API servers are interchangeable, but the database holds state that must stay consistent
Databases are licensed per server, so extra database servers are always too expensive
API servers run in containers, and databases cannot be run in containers at all
Load balancers can only distribute traffic to API servers, never to a database
questions.why: Any API instance can serve any request because the state lives elsewhere, so scaling out is a matter of starting more. Spreading a database means replication lag, failover or sharding, because every copy must agree on the data. Licensing and containers are incidental, and databases can sit behind proxies.
questions.asked: A warm-up; a strong answer adds that scaling up is simpler and often the right first move.

questions.q: Why are sticky sessions (the load balancer pinning each user to one server) usually a stopgap rather than a design?
choices: They force every request through TLS twice, which doubles CPU use
They stop the browser from caching static files between page loads
A server restart logs out its users and the load spreads unevenly
They require every server to share a single database connection
questions.why: Sticky sessions keep state on one server, so a deploy or crash loses those sessions and busy users pile onto whichever server they landed on. Moving session state to Redis, the database or a signed cookie removes the need. TLS, browser caching and connection sharing are unrelated.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand statelessness as the thing that makes scaling out easy.

questions.q: You are moving from one server to several behind a load balancer. Where should login sessions live?
choices: In each server's memory, with the load balancer copying them across
In a shared store such as Redis or the database, or a signed cookie
In a file on the first server, which the other servers read over the network
In the browser's localStorage, which the server reads on each request
questions.why: Any server must be able to recognise any user, so session state goes in a shared store, or in a signed or encrypted cookie the client sends every time. Load balancers do not copy memory, a file on one server is a single point of failure, and the server cannot read localStorage at all.
questions.asked: The first practical consequence of 'make it stateless', asked in almost every scaling discussion.

questions.q: `GET /api/customers/42/orders` takes 900 ms and the database is the bottleneck. What should you do before adding a cache?
choices: Move the orders table to its own database server
Add Redis in front of the query with a one-hour TTL
Read the query plan and add an index on `customer_id`
Rewrite the endpoint to load all orders and filter in memory
questions.why: A slow single-table lookup is usually a missing index, and fixing it makes every caller fast with no invalidation to manage. A cache hides the problem and serves stale orders; a new server is expensive; filtering in memory reads more data, not less.
questions.asked: Interviewers use this to see whether you reach for infrastructure before measuring.

questions.q: Monthly finance reports run heavy aggregate queries against the production database and slow down checkout while they run. What is the usual fix?
choices: Run the reports against a read replica or precomputed summary tables
Increase the command timeout so checkout queries wait for the reports
Rewrite the report queries using an ORM so they generate simpler SQL
Add indexes on every column the reports filter or group by
questions.why: Separate analytical load from transactional load: a replica takes the reads off the primary, and summary tables built incrementally avoid rescanning history. Longer timeouts make checkout slower, not faster. Indexing every column slows writes and rarely helps full-table aggregates much.
questions.asked: A realistic mid-level problem; strong candidates mention replication lag being acceptable for reports.

questions.q: Your build outputs `app.3f9a1c.js` with a content hash in the name. What caching header suits it best?
choices: `Cache-Control: no-store`, so users always get the newest bundle
`Cache-Control: no-cache`, so the CDN checks with the origin each time
`Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`
`Cache-Control: private, max-age=300`, refreshed every five minutes
questions.why: A hashed filename changes whenever the content changes, so the file at that URL never changes and can be cached for a year. New deploys reference new names. `no-store` and `no-cache` throw that away, and `private` stops the CDN from caching it at all.
questions.asked: Checks that you connect build output naming to HTTP caching, which is how static assets get to near-zero cost.

questions.q: Why run at least two instances of the API even when one can handle all the traffic?
choices: Two instances halve the database load compared with one instance
Deploys and crashes then happen without the whole API going down
Load balancers refuse to start with fewer than two healthy targets
Each instance can then cache a different half of the product data
questions.why: With one instance, every deploy, crash or host maintenance is an outage; with two, the load balancer sends traffic to the survivor. Database load depends on requests, not instance count. Load balancers work with one target, and splitting a cache by instance is not the goal.
questions.asked: A basic piece of the scaling picture; the good answer says what the endpoint should and should not check.

questions.q: In a back-of-envelope estimate, 1 million daily users make 10 requests each. Roughly what is the average request rate?
choices: About 12 requests per second
About 115 requests per second
About 1,150 requests per second
About 11,500 requests per second
questions.why: 10 million requests over 86,400 seconds is about 116 per second. Rounding a day to 100,000 seconds is the usual shortcut. Peaks are several times the average, but even 500 per second is well within one database and a few app servers, which is the point of doing the sum.
questions.asked: Interviewers want the arithmetic done out loud, and then the conclusion that this does not need exotic infrastructure.

questions.q: An app records 1 million orders a day at about 1 KB per row. Roughly how much raw table data does a year produce?
choices: About 36 GB
About 365 GB
About 3.6 TB
About 36 TB
questions.why: A million rows at 1 KB is 1 GB a day, so about 365 GB a year before indexes. That fits comfortably on one Postgres or SQL Server instance. The distractors are the same digits off by a factor of ten, which is the mistake people make when they skip writing the units down.
questions.asked: Storage sums decide whether you need partitioning or archiving; showing the units is what earns the credit.

questions.q: In a booking system, what stops two customers from booking the same hairdresser for the same 30-minute slot?
choices: Checking availability in the API before inserting the booking row
A unique constraint on the stylist and slot start time
Disabling the slot in the UI as soon as someone selects it
Refreshing the calendar every few seconds for every open browser
questions.why: Two requests can both pass an availability check before either inserts, so only the database can make the rule hold. A unique index on (stylist_id, slot_start) turns the second insert into an error you map to 409. UI tricks and polling narrow the window but never close it.
questions.asked: The first question in any booking design; the good answer names the race and puts the rule in the database.

questions.q: Bookings can start and end at any minute, so a slot constraint no longer works. How can Postgres reject overlapping bookings for the same room?
choices: A unique index on `(room_id, starts_at, ends_at)`
A check constraint that `ends_at` is after `starts_at`
An exclusion constraint on room and time range using `&&`
A trigger that sleeps briefly before inserting each booking
questions.why: `EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)` over a `tstzrange` rejects any two rows whose ranges overlap for the same room; the `btree_gist` extension allows the equality part. A unique index only catches identical ranges, and a check constraint looks at one row at a time.
questions.asked: Rarely known by juniors; mentioning it, or the SQL Server alternative of a serialisable transaction, stands out.

questions.q: Customers pick a concert seat and then have 10 minutes to pay. How should the temporary hold be modelled?
choices: A hold row with an `expires_at`, ignored by availability queries once it has passed
A timer in the web server's memory that frees the seat after ten minutes
A flag on the seat row that a cron job clears every hour for abandoned carts
A browser `setTimeout` that calls a release endpoint when the time runs out
questions.why: If availability treats expired holds as free, correctness does not depend on any cleanup running on time; a job can delete old rows later. Server timers vanish on restart, an hourly job leaves seats blocked for up to an hour, and a browser timer never fires if the tab closes.
questions.asked: Holds appear in booking, ticketing and checkout designs; interviewers like answers where expiry is data, not a timer.

questions.q: A gym runs a class every Tuesday at 18:00 London time, all year. What should you store for the recurrence?
choices: The UTC time of the first class, adding seven days for each week
The local time 18:00 plus the IANA zone `Europe/London`
The local time 18:00 with a fixed offset of `+01:00`
The server's local time, since the server is in London
questions.why: 18:00 in London is 17:00 UTC in summer and 18:00 UTC in winter, so a UTC start plus seven days drifts by an hour at each clock change, and a fixed offset is wrong for half the year. Store the wall-clock time and the zone and convert each occurrence. The server's zone is an accident of hosting.
questions.asked: Time zones are where booking systems break; the strong answer distinguishes instants (UTC) from future local times.

questions.q: Two shoppers try to buy the last unit of a product at the same moment. Which statement prevents overselling?
choices: `SELECT stock` first, then `UPDATE` to `stock - 1` if it was positive
`UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = @id AND stock >= 1`
`UPDATE ... SET stock = @newStock` using the value the page displayed
`INSERT` a sale row and let a nightly job subtract sales from stock
questions.why: The condition and the decrement happen atomically in one statement, so only one of the two updates affects a row; the other sees zero rows affected and fails the purchase. Read-then-write lets both reads see 1. Writing an absolute value from the page overwrites other sales, and a nightly job sells stock you do not have.
questions.asked: The most common checkout race; interviewers want the atomic conditional update and the 'check rows affected' step.

questions.q: A customer double-clicks "Place order" and two identical `POST /orders` requests arrive. What is the standard server-side protection?
choices: Reject any second order from the same customer within one minute
Disable the button after the first click and rely on the client
Deduplicate orders by comparing basket contents in a nightly job
Accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and replay the first response
questions.why: The client generates a key per checkout attempt; the server stores it with the result and returns the stored result for any repeat. Disabling the button helps but retries and network replays bypass it. A time-window rule blocks legitimate second orders, and a nightly clean-up comes after the card was charged twice.
questions.asked: Idempotency keys come up in payments, webhooks and retries; knowing where the key comes from is the detail they check.

questions.q: The payment provider charged the card, but your server crashed before marking the order paid. How does a well-designed checkout recover?
choices: The customer contacts support, who marks the order paid by hand
The frontend retries the whole checkout, charging the card again
The order stays pending until the provider's webhook or a reconciliation job confirms it
The server marks orders paid before calling the provider, so this cannot happen
questions.why: Treat the order as `pending_payment` and let the provider's signed webhook, backed by a periodic job that asks the provider about stuck payments, move it to paid. Retrying the checkout risks a double charge, marking paid first ships unpaid orders, and manual fixes do not scale.
questions.asked: Tests whether you design for partial failure across two systems, which is the heart of any payments question.

questions.q: An order has `isPaid`, `isShipped` and `isCancelled` booleans, and bugs keep producing orders that are both shipped and cancelled. What design fixes this?
choices: A single status with an explicit list of allowed transitions
A database trigger that logs whenever two flags are both true
More unit tests around each place that sets one of the flags
Separate tables for paid, shipped and cancelled orders
questions.why: Three booleans allow eight combinations, most of them nonsense. One status field plus a transition table (pending to paid, paid to shipped, pending to cancelled) makes invalid states unrepresentable and gives you one place to enforce the rules. Logging and tests detect the bug; they do not prevent it.
questions.asked: State machines are the mid-level answer to 'how would you model an order'; the transition list is what they want to hear.

questions.q: Where does a guest shopper's cart usually live in an e-commerce app?
choices: Only in React state, and it is lost on refresh by design
In a server-side cart keyed by an ID in a cookie, merged at login
In the order table, as an order with status `draft` and no customer
In the CDN cache, keyed by the visitor's IP address
questions.why: A cart row identified by an anonymous cookie survives refreshes and devices sharing the cookie, and can be merged into the customer's cart when they sign in. React state loses it. Draft orders mix carts into order reporting, and IP addresses are shared by many people behind one router.
questions.asked: A practical modelling question; strong answers mention merging and expiring abandoned carts.

questions.q: Two admins open the same product, both edit it, and the second save silently overwrites the first. Which design surfaces the conflict?
choices: Lock the product row for as long as either admin has the form open
Save each field separately so the two edits rarely touch the same column
Include a version number in the form and reject saves whose version is stale
Let the last save win and email both admins a copy of the final product
questions.why: Optimistic concurrency sends the version the user loaded; the update includes `WHERE version = @v`, and zero affected rows means someone else saved first, so you return 409 and show the latest data. Holding a lock while a form is open blocks others for minutes, and field-level saves still lose data on the same field.
questions.asked: The lost-update problem appears in every admin screen; the ETag or row-version answer is the expected one.

questions.q: Why should every outbound HTTP call from your API have an explicit timeout?
choices: A hung dependency would otherwise hold threads and connections indefinitely
HTTP clients refuse to send requests at all when no timeout is configured
Timeouts make the remote server process the request with higher priority
Without one, the response body is not decompressed before it is returned
questions.why: Many clients default to very long or infinite waits, so one stuck provider slowly ties up every request that calls it, and your whole API stops. A timeout turns that into a fast, handleable error. It does not change how the remote side prioritises anything.
questions.asked: The simplest reliability habit and one many juniors skip; interviewers like hearing a concrete number chosen from the provider's latency.

questions.q: Why add random jitter to exponential-backoff retries?
choices: It keeps the total retry time under the client's overall timeout
It lets the server tell retries apart from brand-new requests
It stops many clients that failed together from retrying in lockstep
It shortens the average wait so users get their responses sooner
questions.why: If a dependency blips and a thousand clients all back off 1, 2, 4 seconds exactly, they hit it again in synchronised waves. Randomising each delay spreads the retries out so the dependency can recover. Jitter does not bound total time or mark requests as retries.
questions.asked: A detail that shows you have thought about many clients at once, not one client in isolation.

questions.q: The recommendations service is down. What should the product page do?
choices: Return 503 so the user knows the site is having problems
Render without the recommendations section and log the failure
Retry the recommendations call until it succeeds, then render
Redirect the user to the home page, which does not need recommendations
questions.why: Graceful degradation means a non-essential dependency failing removes its feature, not the page. Failing the whole page or retrying indefinitely lets an optional service take down a core one. Redirecting is still a broken experience.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask which dependencies are essential; the good answer classifies them before choosing behaviour.

questions.q: One slow downstream API ties up every worker thread in your service, so requests that never call it also time out. Which pattern contains this?
choices: A read replica, so slow calls go to a different database
A bulkhead: a separate, capped pool for calls to that API
A larger global thread pool, so there are spare threads
Sticky sessions, so slow users stay on one server only
questions.why: A bulkhead limits how many concurrent calls may go to one dependency, so when it slows down only that feature queues or fails and the rest of the service keeps its capacity. A bigger pool fills up too, just later. Replicas and sticky sessions do not touch outbound calls.
questions.asked: A deeper resilience pattern; naming it alongside timeouts and circuit breakers shows you know how they fit together.

questions.q: What is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe?
choices: Liveness checks the database; readiness checks the web server's port
Liveness runs at startup only; readiness runs on every request
Liveness asks if the process should be restarted; readiness asks if it should get traffic
Liveness is for the load balancer; readiness is for the monitoring dashboard
questions.why: A failed liveness probe tells the orchestrator to restart the container; a failed readiness probe only removes it from the load balancer until it recovers. Putting a database check in liveness means a database blip restarts every instance at once, which is the mistake this distinction prevents.
questions.asked: Common in container-hosted shops; the database-in-liveness trap is the follow-up.

questions.q: What is the difference between a work queue and a publish/subscribe topic?
choices: A queue keeps messages forever; a topic deletes them after an hour
A queue hands each message to one consumer; a topic gives every subscriber a copy
A queue is for events; a topic is for commands aimed at one service
A queue needs a database underneath; a topic runs purely in memory
questions.why: Competing consumers on a queue share the work, so each job runs once. A topic fans out: the email service, the analytics service and the search indexer each get their own copy of `OrderPlaced`. Retention and storage vary by product and are not the distinction.
questions.asked: Basic vocabulary for event-driven designs; the good answer gives one example of each.

questions.q: Which message name is an event rather than a command?
choices: `OrderPlaced`
`ReserveStock`
`SendInvoiceEmail`
`ChargeCard`
questions.why: An event is a past-tense fact that any number of services may react to, and the publisher does not care who listens. The others are imperative commands addressed to one handler that is expected to do the work. Mixing the two up leads to publishers that secretly depend on a particular consumer.
questions.asked: Naming reveals design intent; interviewers use it to check you know who owns the decision in each case.

questions.q: When should a queue consumer acknowledge (delete) a message so that no work is lost?
choices: As soon as it receives the message, before starting the work
After the work and its database changes have been committed
Halfway through, once the message has been parsed and validated
Never; the broker deletes it automatically after the first delivery
questions.why: If the consumer crashes before acknowledging, the broker redelivers and the work is retried; acknowledging first means a crash loses the job. The cost of acknowledging last is occasional duplicates, which is why consumers must be idempotent.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand where at-least-once delivery comes from, not just the phrase.

questions.q: `OrderPlaced` events carry only the order ID, and every consumer calls the orders API for the details. What is the main downside?
choices: The broker cannot deliver messages smaller than a few kilobytes
Consumers see the order as it is now, not as it was, and add load to the API
The event can no longer be retried if the consumer fails the first time
Every consumer must share the orders service's database credentials
questions.why: A thin event forces a callback, so a burst of events becomes a burst of API calls, and a consumer processing late may see a cancelled order instead of the placed one. Fat events carry the facts at the time, at the cost of larger messages and a contract to version. Retries and credentials are unaffected.
questions.asked: A real design trade-off; strong candidates say when each shape is right rather than declaring one correct.

questions.q: Which queue metric best tells you that users are waiting too long for background work?
choices: The total number of messages published to the queue since midnight
The number of consumer instances currently connected
The average size in bytes of messages in the queue
The age of the oldest message still waiting in the queue
questions.why: Oldest-message age measures delay directly: a queue of 10,000 tiny jobs cleared in seconds is fine, while 50 jobs stuck for an hour is not. Throughput, consumer count and message size explain a problem once you have one but do not tell you users are waiting.
questions.asked: Alerting on queue length alone is a common mistake; age is the answer that shows production experience.

questions.q: In SQS, a message's visibility timeout is 30 seconds, but processing sometimes takes 45. What happens?
choices: The broker cancels the consumer's work after 30 seconds
The message becomes visible again and a second consumer processes it too
The message moves straight to the dead-letter queue as a failure
Nothing, because the timeout only applies before the first delivery
questions.why: While a consumer works, the message is hidden; if it is not deleted before the timeout, the broker assumes the consumer died and delivers it again. The fix is a longer timeout or extending it while working, plus idempotency. The broker cannot stop your code, and a single timeout does not dead-letter.
questions.asked: A concrete way duplicates appear even with healthy consumers; it shows hands-on queue experience.

questions.q: The outbox relay publishes a row's event and then crashes before marking the row as sent. Why must consumers still be idempotent?
choices: Because the relay will publish that same event again when it restarts
Because the outbox table may drop the row during the crash
Because the broker reorders messages after any publisher crash
Because the consumer's own database commit could be rolled back
questions.why: The outbox guarantees the event is published at least once, not exactly once: the relay cannot atomically publish and update its own table, so a crash in between means a resend. Committed outbox rows do not disappear, and ordering is a separate concern.
questions.asked: Candidates who think the outbox gives exactly-once are caught here; the good answer pairs it with a deduplicating consumer.

questions.q: Why do most teams use a transactional outbox rather than a distributed transaction across the database and the message broker?
choices: Most brokers do not support two-phase commit, and it couples the two systems
The outbox publishes faster because it skips the database entirely
Distributed transactions are forbidden under most data-protection regulations
An outbox guarantees each consumer processes the message exactly once
questions.why: Two-phase commit needs both sides to take part, and most brokers and cloud queues do not, while those that do make every write wait on both systems. The outbox needs only a local transaction plus a relay. It still writes to the database, and it still delivers at least once.
questions.asked: Shows you know why the pattern exists rather than reciting it.

questions.q: A consumer records each processed message ID in a table, in the same transaction as the work it does. What does this give it?
choices: Faster processing, because the table acts as a cache of results
Ordering, because IDs are processed in the order they were inserted
Backpressure, because the table rejects inserts when it is full
Safe redelivery, because a repeated ID is detected and skipped
questions.why: This is the inbox or idempotent-receiver pattern: if the message comes back, the insert of its ID conflicts and the consumer skips it, and because the ID and the effect commit together there is no gap. It does not order messages or speed anything up.
questions.asked: The practical answer to 'how do you make a consumer idempotent' when the work itself is not naturally idempotent.

questions.q: A nightly clean-up job is scheduled inside the API with a timer, and the API now runs as three instances. What goes wrong?
choices: The job runs three times each night unless one instance is chosen to run it
The job never runs, because timers are disabled behind a load balancer
The job runs once, but on a random instance that may have no database access
The job runs once per request, because each request restarts the timer
questions.why: Each instance has its own timer, so each runs the job. Use a single scheduler (a cron job or hosted scheduler), a distributed lock, or a job library that coordinates through the database. Load balancers do not affect in-process timers.
questions.asked: The first surprise when an app scales out; interviewers look for one concrete coordination mechanism.

questions.q: What is a presigned URL in object storage such as S3 or Azure Blob Storage?
choices: A permanent public link to a file, signed once when it is uploaded
A URL signed by a certificate authority so browsers trust the storage host
A URL that routes each upload through your API so the file can be validated first
A time-limited URL that allows one operation on one object without credentials
questions.why: Your API signs a URL with its own credentials that allows, say, a PUT to one key for 10 minutes; the browser uses it directly. It expires, it is scoped to one object and operation, and the upload bypasses your API rather than passing through it.
questions.asked: The building block for every upload and private-download design; a good answer includes the expiry.

questions.q: Users upload profile photos. Why check the file's actual bytes on the server rather than trusting its extension or `Content-Type`?
choices: Because the client controls both and can label any file as `.jpg`
Because browsers strip the extension from files before upload
Because object storage rejects files whose extension is wrong
Because `Content-Type` is only sent by browsers for files larger than 1 MB
questions.why: The filename and header are whatever the client says, so an HTML or script file can arrive labelled `image/jpeg`. Checking the magic bytes, or better re-encoding the image, confirms what it really is. Browsers do send the name and a type, and storage accepts any bytes.
questions.asked: Upload validation is a common security probe; re-encoding images is the answer that impresses.

questions.q: Why should user-uploaded files be served from a separate domain, such as `usercontent.example.net`, rather than your app's domain?
choices: Browsers download files faster from a domain with no cookies set
Search engines penalise sites that host user-uploaded files on their main domain
Object storage buckets can only be reached through their own domain names
An uploaded HTML or SVG file cannot then run script with your app's cookies
questions.why: If a malicious SVG with a script is served from your origin, it runs with access to your cookies and APIs: stored XSS. A separate registrable domain puts it in a different origin. Sending `Content-Disposition: attachment` and a strict content type are the other layers.
questions.asked: A detail many teams learn after an incident; mentioning it shows security thinking beyond the API.

questions.q: The browser uploads directly to object storage with a presigned URL. How does your app reliably learn the upload finished?
choices: The client calls a confirm endpoint and the server checks the object exists
It polls the bucket every minute, listing all objects to find any new ones
It assumes success once the presigned URL has been issued
The storage service writes the new row into your database directly
questions.why: Issuing a URL proves nothing was uploaded. The usual flow is a confirm call (or a storage event notification) after which the server checks the object's existence and size before marking the record ready. Listing a whole bucket does not scale, and storage cannot write to your database.
questions.asked: Tests whether you have followed a direct upload through to the database, not just drawn the arrow.

questions.q: Uploads go to storage first and are confirmed later, and some users abandon them. How do you stop orphaned files piling up?
choices: Run a monthly job that deletes any object older than thirty days
Delete the file whenever the browser tab closes during the upload
Give every object a public URL so that users can clean up their own abandoned files
Write uploads under a `pending/` prefix and let a lifecycle rule expire them
questions.why: Unconfirmed uploads land under a temporary prefix; confirming copies or moves them to their final key, and a bucket lifecycle rule deletes anything left in `pending/` after a day. Browsers cannot be relied on to report closing, and an age-based sweep of everything would delete real files.
questions.asked: Orphan clean-up is where upload designs quietly cost money; this answer shows you thought past the happy path.

questions.q: Invoices are PDFs in a private bucket. How should a signed-in customer download their own invoice?
choices: Make the bucket public and keep the invoice URLs hard to guess
Check ownership in the API, then redirect to a short-lived presigned GET URL
Email every invoice as an attachment instead of offering downloads
Proxy every byte through the API so the bucket never needs a URL
questions.why: The API makes the authorisation decision, and the storage service does the heavy transfer, with a URL that expires in minutes. Unguessable public URLs leak through logs and forwarding. Proxying works but puts every download on your servers, and email is not access control.
questions.asked: The download half of the presigned-URL pattern; interviewers check the auth check comes first.

questions.q: With direct-to-storage uploads, how do you stop someone uploading a 50 GB file to a URL meant for a profile photo?
choices: Rely on the browser's file input `accept` attribute to limit it
Sign an upload policy with a maximum size, and recheck the size on confirm
Scan the bucket nightly and delete any file larger than 5 MB
Set a very short URL expiry so that a large upload cannot possibly finish in time
questions.why: An S3 presigned POST can carry a `content-length-range` condition, and Azure SAS uploads can be checked the same way at confirmation, so oversized uploads are rejected or discarded before they are used. `accept` is a client hint, a nightly scan pays for the storage first, and expiry applies to starting the request.
questions.asked: The follow-up once you propose presigned uploads; it checks you know you gave up the API as a gatekeeper.

questions.q: Why is `WHERE name LIKE '%phone%'` slow on a large table even with an index on `name`?
choices: A leading wildcard means a B-tree index cannot narrow where to start
`LIKE` is always evaluated in the application, not the database
The index is ignored because `name` is a text column, not a number
Wildcard queries take a table lock that blocks other readers while they scan it
questions.why: A B-tree is sorted by the value's prefix, so `LIKE 'phone%'` can seek but `'%phone%'` must scan every row. Trigram indexes or full-text search are the fixes. Text columns index fine, and a read does not lock the table.
questions.asked: The usual starting point of a search discussion; the good answer immediately names an alternative.

questions.q: In Postgres, what does full-text search with a `tsvector` column and a GIN index give you over `ILIKE`?
choices: Matching word forms such as `running` for `run`, with ranking
Fuzzy matching of typos such as `phnoe` to `phone`
Exact substring matches that are case-sensitive
Search across every table in the database without naming columns
questions.why: Full-text search tokenises and stems text in a language configuration, so words match by root, and `ts_rank` orders results; the GIN index makes it fast. It does not tolerate typos, which is what the `pg_trgm` extension is for, and it only searches the columns you build the vector from.
questions.asked: Knowing what built-in search can do stops you proposing Elasticsearch for a 50,000-row table.

questions.q: Users misspell product names in a Postgres-backed app with 200,000 products. What adds typo tolerance without a separate search service?
choices: A `pg_trgm` GIN index with `similarity()` or the `%` operator
A B-tree index on `lower(name)` with an equality comparison
A materialised view that stores every name in upper case
A `tsvector` column using the `simple` text search configuration
questions.why: Trigram similarity compares overlapping three-character chunks, so `iphnoe` still scores close to `iphone`, and the GIN index keeps it fast; it also accelerates `ILIKE '%x%'`. Case-folding and `simple` full-text configurations only match exact words.
questions.asked: A practical 'small-scale search' answer that shows you know the database's own tools.

questions.q: You add OpenSearch for product search. How is its index usually kept up to date with the database?
choices: The API writes to OpenSearch and the database in one transaction
OpenSearch reads the database tables directly over a connector on every search query
A developer rebuilds the index by hand after each product change
Change events feed an indexer that updates documents, accepting a short lag
questions.why: The database stays the source of truth; an outbox event or change-data-capture stream drives an indexer, so search is eventually consistent, and a full reindex job covers drift. There is no shared transaction between the two, and OpenSearch does not query your database.
questions.asked: Interviewers want the sync mechanism and the admission that search can be seconds behind.

questions.q: In a multi-tenant app using a search engine, how do you stop one tenant's documents appearing in another's search results?
choices: Rely on each tenant using different words in their documents
Give each tenant a different ranking formula for results
Hide the results in the frontend whenever their tenant does not match the user
Store `tenant_id` on every document and filter on it in every query
questions.why: Search indexes do not inherit your database's row-level rules, so tenancy must be indexed and enforced as a filter on every query, ideally in one shared query builder. Filtering in the frontend still sends the data to the browser.
questions.asked: A common leak when search is bolted on late; it checks you carry isolation into every data store.

questions.q: What are SPF, DKIM and DMARC for?
choices: Encrypting email in transit between mail servers
Proving your domain authorised the mail, so it avoids spam folders
Tracking whether a recipient opened or clicked the email
Compressing attachments so they fit provider size limits
questions.why: SPF lists which servers may send for your domain, DKIM signs messages, and DMARC tells receivers what to do when those checks fail. Without them, transactional email lands in spam or is rejected. Transport encryption is TLS, and open tracking is a pixel.
questions.asked: Every app sends email; knowing why it goes to spam is a sign you have set one up.

questions.q: Why do teams send marketing email from a different subdomain or stream than password resets and receipts?
choices: Marketing email needs a different template language
Receipts must legally be sent from the company's primary registered domain
So marketing can be sent without SPF and DKIM records
So spam complaints about marketing do not hurt transactional delivery
questions.why: Mailbox providers track reputation per sending domain and IP. Marketing draws unsubscribes and complaints; if it shares a reputation with password resets, those start landing in spam. Both streams still need authentication.
questions.asked: A production detail that shows you think of email as infrastructure rather than a function call.

questions.q: A user turns off comment notification emails while 200 are already queued for them. Where should the preference be checked?
choices: When the comment is created, before the job is queued
In the email template, by hiding the body text
In the email provider's dashboard, by the support team
When each job runs, just before the email is sent
questions.why: Checking at send time respects a change made after the job was queued; checking only at enqueue sends 200 emails the user just refused. Checking at both points is fine, but the send-time check is the one that makes the setting trustworthy.
questions.asked: Timing bugs like this generate complaints and unsubscribes; interviewers like the send-time answer.

questions.q: An in-app notifications table has `user_id` and a nullable `read_at`. Which index best supports the unread badge count in Postgres?
choices: A single-column index on `read_at` alone
A composite index on `(created_at, user_id)`
A partial index on `(user_id)` where `read_at IS NULL`
A unique index on `(user_id, read_at)` pair
questions.why: The badge query is `WHERE user_id = $1 AND read_at IS NULL`; a partial index contains only unread rows, so it stays small as history grows. An index on `read_at` does not narrow by user, `created_at` first cannot seek on user, and a unique constraint would forbid two unread notifications.
questions.asked: Unread counts run on every page load; a targeted index is the difference between cheap and painful.

questions.q: Why batch frequent notifications, such as comments on a busy thread, into a periodic digest email?
choices: One email an hour beats forty, and cuts unsubscribes and sending cost
Digests bypass spam filters that block individual messages
Email providers refuse to deliver more than one message per recipient per hour
Digests let you skip storing the individual notifications
questions.why: Forty separate emails trains users to unsubscribe or mark you as spam, which damages delivery for everyone. A digest collects pending items and sends a summary on a schedule. It still needs the stored notifications to build from, and providers do not impose that limit.
questions.asked: Shows product sense in a system design answer, which interviewers value at mid-level.

questions.q: The email provider reports a hard bounce for a customer's address. What should the app do?
choices: Retry the same email every hour until it is delivered
Add the address to a suppression list and stop sending to it
Delete the customer's account because the email is invalid
Switch to sending from a different email provider for that user
questions.why: A hard bounce means the address does not exist, and continuing to send to it damages your sender reputation. Suppress it and prompt the user to update their address in the app. Retrying makes it worse, and deleting the account is out of proportion.
questions.asked: A small operational question that separates people who have run email in production.

questions.q: Users should see new notifications in an open tab without refreshing, and the browser never sends anything back on that channel. What fits best?
choices: An email with a link that reloads the notifications page
Long polling every 100 milliseconds from each open tab
A WebSocket, because it is the only mechanism that lets a server push to a tab
Server-Sent Events from an endpoint that streams notifications
questions.why: Server-Sent Events are a one-way stream over ordinary HTTP with automatic reconnection, which matches a notification feed. WebSockets also work but are two-way, which you do not need, and are not the only option. Polling ten times a second is wasteful.
questions.asked: Checks you pick the simplest transport that fits rather than defaulting to WebSockets.

questions.q: Why do webhook signature schemes include a timestamp in the signed payload?
choices: So the receiver can sort webhooks into the order they were sent
So a captured request cannot be replayed later and still verify
So the receiver knows which secret to use during key rotation
So the sender can measure how long the receiver took to respond
questions.why: An HMAC alone proves the payload came from the sender but not when; an attacker who captures one request could resend it forever. Including the timestamp in the signature and rejecting anything older than a few minutes closes that. Ordering and key rotation are handled separately.
questions.asked: A follow-up to 'how do you verify a webhook'; it checks you understand what a signature does not prove.

questions.q: What should an endpoint that receives payment webhooks do before returning its response?
choices: Fulfil the whole order, including emails, so nothing is missed
Verify the signature, store the event, and return 2xx quickly
Call the provider's API three times to confirm the event is real
Return 202 without checking anything, then validate it later
questions.why: Providers time out slow receivers and retry, so the endpoint verifies, records the event (deduplicated by its ID) and hands the work to a background job. Doing all the work inline invites timeouts and duplicate fulfilment; skipping verification means storing forged events.
questions.asked: The standard receive-side shape; a good answer mentions deduplication by event ID.

questions.q: In a multi-tenant API, where should the current tenant ID come from?
choices: An `X-Tenant-Id` header the frontend sends with each request
The authenticated user's token or session, checked on the server
A query-string parameter, so links can be shared between tenants
The `tenant_id` field in the JSON body of each write request
questions.why: Anything the client sends can be changed, so a header, parameter or body field lets a user read another tenant's data by editing one value. The tenant comes from the identity the server authenticated, or from a subdomain that is then checked against that identity.
questions.asked: The most basic multi-tenant security check; getting it wrong is a whole class of breach.

questions.q: Postgres row-level security reads the tenant from a session variable, and connections are pooled. How should the variable be set?
choices: With `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id` inside each request's transaction
With `SET app.tenant_id` once when the pool opens each connection
In the connection string, with one pool shared by all tenants
In a column default, so each insert picks up the right tenant
questions.why: `SET LOCAL` lasts only until the transaction ends, so a pooled connection cannot carry one request's tenant into the next. A plain `SET` persists on the connection, which is exactly how tenant data leaks under pooling. A shared connection string cannot hold per-request values.
questions.asked: RLS is a strong answer only if you know this pitfall; interviewers who use it will ask.

questions.q: In a shared-schema multi-tenant app, each tenant's users need unique email addresses. Which constraint is right?
choices: `UNIQUE (email)` across the whole users table
`UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)` on the users table
`UNIQUE (tenant_id)` on the users table
No constraint; check for duplicates in the API
questions.why: The same person may belong to two customer organisations, so email is unique within a tenant, not globally. A global constraint blocks that; unique `tenant_id` allows one user per tenant; an API check alone loses to concurrent inserts.
questions.asked: Small, but it shows you carry tenancy into constraints and indexes, not just queries.

questions.q: What keeps a modular monolith modular as it grows?
choices: Deploying each module as its own separate container behind the same public domain
All modules share one large `Services` folder so code is easy to find
Every module uses a different programming language and framework
Modules call each other only through public interfaces, never each other's tables
questions.why: The boundary is the rule that module A never reaches into module B's data or internals; enforce it with project references, internal visibility or architecture tests. Separate containers make it a distributed system. Language choice is irrelevant, and one shared folder is how boundaries disappear.
questions.asked: Everyone says 'modular monolith'; interviewers want to hear how the modularity is enforced.

questions.q: Image processing in your monolith is CPU-heavy and slows web requests during busy periods. What is the usual first step?
choices: Run the same codebase as a separate worker process that consumes a queue
Extract image processing into a microservice with its own database
