Buy a larger server so the web requests have more CPU to share with the image work
Move image processing into the browser using WebAssembly
questions.why: The same code deployed in a worker role, scaled separately and fed by a queue, isolates the CPU load without a new service boundary, a new database or network contracts. A bigger server postpones the problem. A microservice is a much larger change for the same isolation.
questions.asked: The 'scale the monolith before splitting it' answer that interviewers want to hear before microservices come up.

questions.q: Your app soft-deletes users with a `deleted_at` column. A user makes a GDPR erasure request. What is needed?
choices: Nothing more, because soft-deleted rows are hidden from queries
Setting `deleted_at` again, with a note of the request date
Actually deleting or anonymising their personal data, including backups over time
Moving their row to an archive table that only admins can read
questions.why: Soft delete hides data; it does not erase it. Erasure means removing or irreversibly anonymising the personal fields, cascading to related tables and ageing out of backups by your retention policy. An archive table still holds the data.
questions.asked: Soft delete is common, and interviewers use this to check you know its limits.

questions.q: An auditor asks who changed a product's price last March and what it was before. Which design can answer?
choices: An `updated_at` column on the products table
Application logs kept for the default seven days
An append-only audit table written in the same transaction as the change
A nightly backup of the products table kept for a month
questions.why: An audit row per change records who, when, and the old and new values, and writing it in the same transaction means it cannot be skipped. `updated_at` keeps only the latest time, logs expire and are not structured for this, and a month of backups cannot reach last March.
questions.asked: Audit trails appear in most business CRUD systems; the same-transaction detail is the mark of a good answer.

questions.q: In a system design interview, what should you do in the first five minutes?
choices: Draw the full architecture so the interviewer sees your plan early
Pick the database and justify it before discussing anything else
List the microservices you would build and how they communicate
Clarify the core features, users and rough scale before drawing
questions.why: The design depends on what the system must do and how big it is: 500 users and 5 million users lead to different answers. Drawing or choosing technology first means designing for a problem you have not confirmed, which interviewers mark down even if the diagram is good.
questions.asked: Interviewers score the requirements step explicitly; skipping it is the most common way to fail the round.

questions.q: For a booking system, which of these is a non-functional requirement?
choices: Customers can cancel any booking free of charge up to 24 hours before it starts
Staff can see every booking for their location on one screen
Availability searches return within 300 ms at the 95th percentile
Customers receive a confirmation email after each booking
questions.why: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, availability and security rather than features. Cancellation, a staff view and confirmation emails are all things the system does, so they are functional requirements.
questions.asked: A vocabulary check at the start of the design round; strong answers volunteer two or three NFRs unprompted.

questions.q: Roughly how much downtime per month does a 99.9% availability target allow?
choices: About 4.3 minutes
About 43 minutes
About 7 hours
About 3 days
questions.why: 0.1% of a 30-day month (43,200 minutes) is about 43 minutes. 99.99% allows about 4 minutes, and 99% about 7 hours. Knowing these tells you whether a manual deploy with a few minutes of downtime is compatible with the target.
questions.asked: Availability numbers anchor the reliability part of a design discussion; interviewers like the conversion done quickly.

questions.q: What does a recovery point objective (RPO) of one hour mean?
choices: The system must be back online within one hour of an outage
Backups must be restored and tested at least once an hour
Losing up to one hour of data in a disaster is acceptable
Monitoring must detect any outage within one hour
questions.why: RPO is how much recent data you can afford to lose, which sets how often you back up or replicate. How quickly you must be running again is the recovery time objective (RTO), the usual mix-up.
questions.asked: RPO and RTO come up when backups are discussed; defining both correctly is enough at mid-level.

questions.q: Nightly database backups have run for a year but have never been restored. What is the risk?
choices: The backups use more storage each night than the database itself
Nobody knows whether they restore, or how long a restore takes
Old backups expire automatically after 90 days on most providers
Backups taken at night miss data written in the daytime
questions.why: A backup is only proven by a restore: files can be corrupt, incomplete or missing permissions, and nobody has measured the recovery time. A scheduled test restore into a scratch environment turns an assumption into evidence. Retention and timing are separate settings.
questions.asked: A reliability habit interviewers like to hear, because many teams discover the problem during a real outage.

questions.q: Why should a checkout store money as `decimal(12,2)` or integer pence rather than a floating-point type?
choices: Floating-point types cannot store negative numbers such as refunds
Decimal columns use less disk space than floating-point columns
Binary floating point cannot represent values like 0.10 exactly
Floating-point columns cannot be indexed in most databases
questions.why: 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so sums of prices drift by fractions of a penny and totals fail to reconcile. Decimal and integer minor units are exact. Floats can be negative and can be indexed, and size is not the reason.
questions.asked: A classic data-modelling check for anything involving payments.

questions.q: Why does an order line store the unit price at the time of purchase instead of joining to the product's current price?
choices: Joins between orders and products are too slow to run on every order page
Storing it again lets the customer edit the price during checkout
Prices are stored in a different database from orders for security
The product's price will change, but what the customer paid must not
questions.why: An order is a historical record: invoices, refunds and reports must reflect what was charged, not today's price. The same applies to product names and tax rates. Join cost is not the reason, and the customer never sets the price.
questions.asked: A small modelling question that shows whether you think about data over time.

questions.q: After each deploy the in-memory caches start empty and the database spikes for a few minutes. What does cache warming do?
choices: Raises every entry's TTL so the caches empty less often during the day
Preloads the hottest keys before an instance starts taking traffic
Moves the cache into the database so it survives deploys automatically
Sends every request to the old version until its cache has expired
questions.why: A warm-up step loads known-hot keys (top products, reference data) before the instance reports ready, so the first real requests hit the cache. Longer TTLs do nothing for an empty cache, putting the cache in the database defeats it, and routing to the old version is a blue-green concern.
questions.asked: Basic infrastructure vocabulary; a good answer mentions which responses must never be cached there.

questions.q: You replace `/images/logo.png` (no hash in the name) and users still see the old logo from the CDN. What fixes it now and in future?
choices: Restart the origin server so that the CDN notices the change
Delete the file and upload it again under the same name
Purge that path now, and use hashed filenames from now on
Ask users to clear their browser caches and reload
questions.why: A purge tells the CDN to drop its cached copy immediately; content-hashed names mean future changes get a new URL and never need a purge. The CDN does not watch your origin, reuploading changes nothing it has cached, and browser clearing cannot be relied on.
questions.asked: Checks you know the two tools for stale CDN content and prefer the one that needs no manual step.

questions.q: What does "single point of failure" mean when reviewing a design diagram?
choices: A component with no redundancy whose failure takes the system down
The component that fails most often according to the monitoring dashboards
A service that is shared by more than one team in the company
The first component a request passes through, usually the DNS
questions.why: If one box on the diagram fails and everything stops, and there is no second one to take over, it is a single point of failure. The usual fixes are a second instance, a managed service with failover, or accepting the risk explicitly. How often it fails or who owns it is a separate question.
questions.asked: Interviewers often ask 'what are the single points of failure here?' of your own diagram.

questions.q: What is sharding a database?
choices: Copying the whole database to several read replicas
Compressing large columns so the table fits in memory
Moving old rows from a large table into a cheaper archive table on a schedule
Splitting rows across several databases by a key such as tenant ID
questions.why: Each shard holds a subset of the rows and the app, or a router, picks the shard from the key. It spreads writes as well as reads, at the cost of cross-shard queries and rebalancing. Replicas copy everything, and archiving and compression do not distribute load.
questions.asked: Expected vocabulary; the strong answer adds that most CRUD apps never need it.

questions.q: On a flash-sale day, orders spike to ten times normal for an hour. How does sending confirmation emails through a queue help?
choices: The queue absorbs the spike and workers drain it at a steady rate
The queue sends the emails faster than the provider normally allows
The queue stops customers placing orders once it gets too long
The queue merges duplicate emails into one per customer
questions.why: A queue decouples the rate work arrives from the rate it is done: checkout stays fast and emails go out a few minutes later as workers catch up. It does not make the email provider faster, throttle checkout, or deduplicate by itself.
questions.asked: The 'why a queue' answer in plain terms; interviewers want load levelling, not buzzwords.

questions.q: Why do web apps use a database connection pool?
choices: Opening a new connection per query costs time, and databases limit connections
The pool caches query results so repeated queries skip the database
The pool splits each query across several connections so its parts run in parallel
Databases reject queries sent on connections that are not pooled
questions.why: Connecting involves a network handshake, authentication and server-side setup, and each connection costs the server memory, so apps reuse a small set. The pool does not cache results or parallelise a single query.
questions.asked: A foundation for the 'we scaled out and the database refused connections' question.

questions.q: What does it mean that search results are eventually consistent with the database?
choices: Search results are sometimes wrong and never corrected
The database waits for the search index before committing
Search only returns new results after the nightly index rebuild has run
A change appears in search after a short delay, not instantly
questions.why: Eventual consistency means that without new writes the copies converge; for a moment after saving, search may show the old version. The database does not wait for the index, and a correct pipeline converges in seconds, not overnight.
questions.asked: The term comes up with replicas, caches and search; interviewers want a plain-English definition.

questions.q: A user edits a document's title and the list page, served from an eventually consistent search index, still shows the old title. What is the usual UI approach?
choices: Update the item in the UI from the save response, not the index
Block the save request until the search index confirms the update
Reload the list page every second until the new title appears
Tell users that edits take up to a day to show in lists
questions.why: The write response already contains the new state, so the client updates its cache or list from that, and the index catches up in the background. Blocking couples the save to the index, and polling or warnings make a short lag feel like a bug.
questions.asked: Tests whether you connect backend consistency choices to what the user sees.

questions.q: A post shows `comment_count`, and counting comments on every page view is slow. What is the usual design?
choices: Cache the whole page for a day so that the expensive count query rarely runs at all
Estimate the count from the table's total row statistics
Count comments in the browser after loading them all
Store a counter on the post, updated in the same transaction as each comment
questions.why: A denormalised counter updated atomically (`SET comment_count = comment_count + 1`) with the insert is cheap to read and stays correct. A day-long cache shows stale counts, loading every comment is the slow part you wanted to avoid, and table statistics are not per post.
questions.asked: Denormalisation with a clear consistency rule is a common mid-level design move.

questions.q: An `events` table grows by 50 million rows a month, and queries only touch the last 90 days. What helps most long-term?
choices: Add a second index on every column that appears in any of the queries' `WHERE` clauses
Increase the database server's RAM each time queries slow down
Move older rows to an archive table or cold storage on a schedule
Switch the table's primary key from integers to UUIDs
questions.why: Archiving keeps the hot table small, so its indexes fit in memory and maintenance stays fast, while old data remains available elsewhere. More indexes slow the heavy insert load, RAM only postpones the problem, and key type does not change table size meaningfully.
questions.asked: Data growth is where CRUD systems actually slow down; this checks you plan for it.

questions.q: A sold-out class keeps a waitlist. When a place frees up, what is the fair and robust design?
choices: Email everyone on the waitlist at once and let whoever clicks first take the free place
Offer the place to the next person with a timed hold, then move on if unclaimed
Add the next person automatically and charge their saved card
Leave the place empty until staff review the waitlist manually
questions.why: A hold for the next person in line, with an expiry, respects order and does not charge anyone without consent; when it expires the offer moves down the list. Emailing everyone creates a race and disappointment, auto-charging surprises people, and manual review leaves places unfilled.
questions.asked: A realistic booking twist that tests whether you reuse the hold pattern.

questions.q: A discount code may be used at most 100 times, and many shoppers apply it at once. Which update enforces the limit?
choices: Read `used` in the API, and if it is under 100, write `used + 1`
Store the count in Redis without expiry and check it before checkout
Count redemptions in a nightly job and disable the code if it passed 100
`UPDATE coupons SET used = used + 1 WHERE code = @c AND used < 100`
questions.why: The check and increment happen in one atomic statement, so the 101st update affects zero rows and that checkout is refused. Read-then-write lets several requests see 99 at once. A nightly job allows unlimited overuse in the meantime, and a separate Redis check still races with the write.
questions.asked: The same atomic-conditional-update idea as stock, in a different costume; interviewers check you recognise it.

questions.q: A product's price rises while it sits in a customer's cart. What should checkout do?
choices: Charge the old price, because the customer added the item to the cart at that price
Charge the new price silently, because it is the current price
Reprice at checkout and show the customer the change before paying
Remove the item from the cart and ask them to add it again
questions.why: The server is the source of truth for prices at the moment of purchase, and the customer must see what they will pay before paying. Honouring stale prices is a business decision, not a default. Silent changes cause chargebacks, and removing the item is needlessly hostile.
questions.asked: Shows you think about the cart as a snapshot that must be revalidated.

questions.q: An email job may be retried after a crash. How do you avoid sending the same order confirmation twice?
choices: Send the email first, and record `confirmation_sent_at` on the order only if the send throws an error
Check and set `confirmation_sent_at` on the order, and pass the provider an idempotency key
Retry the job only once, so a second email is at worst sent one time
Ask the email provider to discard any message with an identical subject
questions.why: Record that the send happened and check it before sending, and where the provider supports an idempotency key, use one so a crash between sending and recording does not double-send. Limiting retries still duplicates, and subject-based deduplication would drop legitimate emails.
questions.asked: Every at-least-once consumer needs this; interviewers look for the crash-between-steps reasoning.

questions.q: Why do public APIs rate-limit per client key rather than with one global limit?
choices: One misbehaving client should not use up capacity everyone else needs
A single global limit is impossible to implement correctly across several servers
Per-key limits let clients see each other's usage in the headers
A global limit would block health checks from the load balancer
questions.why: Per-key limits isolate clients: a runaway script gets 429 responses while everyone else is unaffected. A global limit punishes all users for one client's behaviour. Distributed global limits are possible with a shared store, and usage headers only show your own quota.
questions.asked: Fairness is the point interviewers want; the follow-up is where the counters live.

questions.q: Users can request page 5,000 of search results, and deep pages are slow. What do most products do?
choices: Precompute every page of results and store them in the cache
Rebuild the search index nightly so that deep pages are faster
Return every matching result on one page and let the browser paginate
Cap how deep users can page and push them to refine the search
questions.why: Deep offset pagination makes the engine collect and discard thousands of results, and nobody reads page 5,000. Capping depth (most search engines have a limit) and offering filters is the practical answer. Precomputing every page and returning everything both scale with the result count.
questions.asked: A product-minded answer to a performance question, which is what interviewers want from mid-level.

questions.q: Uploaded photos need three sizes of thumbnail. Why generate them in a background job at upload time rather than on the first request for each size?
choices: Browsers cannot display images that were generated on demand by an image service
Object storage cannot store more than one version of a file
The first viewer would wait for resizing, and bursts would pile up CPU on the web tier
Generating on request would require the original uploads to be publicly readable by anyone
questions.why: On-demand generation puts slow CPU work in the request path, and a popular new upload triggers many simultaneous resizes. A job after upload keeps requests fast. On-demand resizing through an image CDN is also valid, but it moves the work off your servers rather than onto them.
questions.asked: Tests whether you keep CPU-heavy work out of requests by default.

questions.q: What is an error budget, given an SLO of 99.9% successful requests?
choices: The 0.1% of requests that may fail before reliability work takes priority
The money set aside each quarter for refunding or crediting customers after outages
The number of bugs a team may leave open before a release is blocked
The retry allowance each client gets before its requests are rejected
questions.why: The error budget is the failure the SLO allows. While it remains, the team can ship quickly; once it is spent, work shifts to reliability. It is not a finance, bug-count or rate-limiting concept.
questions.asked: SLO vocabulary shows up in teams with an on-call rota; a crisp definition is enough.

questions.q: You need to rename the `customers.fullname` column to `display_name` while old and new app versions run side by side during a rolling deploy. What is the safe sequence?
choices: Rename the column in one migration, then deploy the new app version
Deploy the new app version first, then rename the column once all traffic has moved to it
Take the site offline for five minutes and do both changes together
Add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old one
questions.why: Expand and contract keeps the schema compatible with both app versions at every step. Renaming first breaks the old instances still reading `fullname`; deploying first breaks the new ones. Downtime works but is what zero-downtime deploys exist to avoid.
questions.asked: Schema changes during rolling deploys are a mid-to-senior filter; naming expand-and-contract is the key.

questions.q: A trip booking reserves a flight, then a hotel, through two different providers, and the hotel fails. There is no shared transaction. What is the usual pattern?
choices: Retry the hotel forever, since the flight is already booked
Leave the flight booked and email the customer to find a hotel
Wrap both calls in a database transaction and roll it back
Run a compensating action that cancels the flight booking
questions.why: A saga is a sequence of local steps, each with a compensating action that undoes it when a later step fails. A database transaction cannot roll back an external provider's booking. Retrying forever never finishes, and leaving half a trip booked hands the failure to the customer.
questions.asked: Sagas come up whenever two external systems must change together; interviewers want 'compensate', not 'rollback'.

questions.q: In a social feature, one account has 2 million followers. Why do many designs build that account's posts into feeds at read time rather than writing into every follower's feed?
choices: Reading at request time is always faster than a precomputed feed
Precomputed feeds cannot be paginated beyond the first page
Accounts with many followers cannot be stored in a relational database
Writing one post into 2 million feeds is a huge, slow burst of writes
questions.why: Fan-out on write suits normal accounts because reads become a cheap lookup, but a celebrity post multiplies into millions of writes. The hybrid merges those few accounts' posts in at read time. Neither approach is always faster, and both can be stored and paginated normally.
questions.asked: The classic feed trade-off; mid-level candidates who explain the hybrid stand out.

questions.q: A Postgres `events` table is partitioned by month. What does that make cheap that a single table does not?
choices: Dropping a whole old month with one quick detach or drop
Updating rows across every month in a single statement
Joining events to users without using any index
Enforcing a unique constraint across all months without the partition key
questions.why: Removing an old partition is a metadata operation, while deleting 50 million rows from one table is slow, bloats it and needs vacuuming. Queries filtered by date also skip irrelevant partitions. Cross-partition updates are not cheaper, and unique constraints must include the partition key.
questions.asked: A deeper database question for designs with high-volume append-only data.

questions.q: Each enterprise tenant has its own database, 300 in total. What becomes the hardest part of shipping a schema change?
choices: Writing the migration SQL, which must differ for each tenant
Paying for extra licences because each migration counts as a new database
Getting written approval from every tenant's administrator before their database can change
Running it across every database, tracking failures, and supporting mixed versions meanwhile
questions.why: The same migration must run 300 times; some will fail or lag, so you need tooling to track per-database versions and retry, and the app must work against both old and new schemas until all are done. The SQL is the same everywhere, and licences are not tied to migrations.
questions.asked: The operational cost of database-per-tenant, which interviewers want named before you propose it.

questions.q: An API supports `ETag` and `If-None-Match`, and a client's cached copy is still current. What does the conditional request save?
choices: All server work, because the server skips the handler entirely
The TLS handshake, because the connection is reused automatically
Transferring the body, although the server may still build the response
Nothing, because HTTP clients must always download the full body on every request
questions.why: A 304 carries no body, which saves bandwidth and client parsing. Unless the ETag can be checked cheaply, for example from a version column, the server still loads the data and hashes the response to compare. Connection reuse is unrelated.
questions.asked: Distinguishes people who know what conditional requests actually optimise; the version-column trick is a strong follow-up.

questions.q: Two identical `POST /orders` requests with the same idempotency key arrive 50 ms apart, while the first is still processing. What should the server do with the second?
choices: Return 409 or wait, because a request with that key is in progress
Process it too, since the first has not stored a response yet
Return the 201 response of the first request, which has not finished
Silently drop it, returning no response so the client times out
questions.why: The server should claim the key atomically, for example with a unique insert, before doing the work; a concurrent duplicate sees the key in progress and gets 409 (or waits for the stored result). Processing it charges twice, there is no response to replay yet, and dropping it leaves the client guessing.
questions.asked: The concurrency edge of idempotency keys, which separates people who have implemented them.

questions.q: When sketching a CRUD system's data model in the design round, what should you do first?
choices: Write the full SQL schema with every column and type
Name the main entities, their relationships, and the hot queries
Choose between SQL and NoSQL databases before thinking about any of the entities
Design the caching layer so the model fits the cache
questions.why: Entities, relationships and the queries that run most often drive tables, keys and indexes; that is enough detail for the round. Full DDL wastes time, the database choice follows from the data, and caching comes after you know what is slow.
questions.asked: Interviewers want the model at the right level of detail; over-specifying is a common time sink.

questions.q: Your design has one API, one Postgres primary and one Redis. The interviewer asks how it survives the primary failing. What is a reasonable mid-level answer?
choices: A managed database with a standby that fails over automatically
Redis takes over as the primary database until Postgres returns
The API buffers writes in memory until the primary comes back
Nothing is needed, because relational databases do not fail
questions.why: Managed Postgres and SQL Server offerings keep a synchronous or near-synchronous standby and promote it in a minute or two, which is the standard answer. Redis is not a substitute primary, in-memory buffering loses writes on restart, and databases certainly fail.
questions.asked: Checks you can close a single-point-of-failure gap without over-engineering.

questions.q: What is a reasonable first design for a CRUD app expected to serve 50,000 users in its first year?
choices: One API behind a load balancer, one managed relational database, and a queue for background jobs
Separate microservices for users, orders and billing, each with its own database and deploy pipeline
A globally distributed database with active-active writes across three regions
A serverless function for every endpoint, sharing a document database
questions.why: At this scale a stateless API with two or more instances, a managed database with a standby, and a job queue covers load and reliability with the least operational work. Microservices, multi-region writes and per-endpoint functions add cost and failure modes the numbers do not justify.
questions.asked: Interviewers reward matching the design to the stated scale rather than to famous companies.

questions.q: A partner integration sends updates by polling your API every 5 seconds for 20,000 records. What design change removes most of that load?
choices: Add a larger page size so that the partner needs fewer requests for each poll cycle
Ask the partner to poll every second so each response is smaller
Cache the full response for 5 seconds so each poll is served from Redis
Let the partner fetch only records changed since a cursor, or push webhooks
questions.why: Incremental sync (`?updatedSince=` or a change cursor) returns only what changed, and webhooks remove polling entirely. Bigger pages and caching still ship 20,000 records every few seconds, and more frequent polling adds requests.
questions.asked: A common integration design problem; the change-cursor answer shows you think about data volume, not just request count.

questions.q: A booking confirmation is viewed by a traveller whose laptop is set to a different time zone from the hotel. Which time zone should check-in be shown in?
choices: The traveller's browser zone, converted automatically
UTC, so that every reader sees the identical value
The hotel's zone, labelled, since that is where it happens
The server's zone, since the booking was made there
questions.why: A check-in time is a local event at the hotel, so show it in the hotel's zone and say which zone it is. Converting to the viewer's zone produces times that are wrong on arrival, UTC is meaningless to most guests, and the server's zone is an accident of hosting.
questions.asked: Time-zone display is a frequent real bug in booking products; interviewers like the 'where does the event happen' rule.

questions.q: Why does a webhook-events table usually have a unique constraint on `(provider, event_id)`?
choices: So the provider can look up which events you have processed
So events are always processed in the order they were created
So events from different providers are stored in separate tables
So a retried delivery of the same event is rejected as a duplicate
questions.why: Providers retry webhooks when they do not get a timely 2xx, so the same event can arrive several times; inserting it under a unique key makes the second insert fail and the handler skip it. The constraint does not order events or split tables, and the provider cannot see your database.
questions.asked: The concrete mechanism behind 'de-duplicate webhooks', which interviewers ask for after you say the phrase.
